notes.7: Set of the two permitted sort directions.
notes.14: Parameters come straight from the HTTP query string via a controller.
notes.16: Direction is upper-cased and falls back to ASC if not in the set.
notes.17: Clamps the requested row limit to the range 1..100.
notes.18: Start of the SQL text; the category is a bound placeholder.
notes.19: Appends the sort column and direction to the query.
notes.22: Compiles the assembled SQL as a prepared statement.
notes.23: Binds the category value to the first placeholder.

options.label: The limit value is concatenated into the SQL, so an attacker can supply a negative number to dump the whole table.
options.whyWrong: The limit is clamped to 1..100 and is an int, so it cannot carry SQL text.

options.label: The category parameter is bound with setString, which fails to stop injection for string columns.
options.whyWrong: Bound parameters are the correct defense; category is not interpolated into the SQL.

options.label: The sortBy string is concatenated into the SQL unvalidated. A prepared statement cannot protect it, so attacker-controlled SQL expressions become part of the ORDER BY clause.
options.whyWrong: This is the mechanism: the column name is never bound or checked against an allowlist.

options.label: The direction check uses toUpperCase(), which is locale-sensitive and lets crafted keywords bypass the allowlist.
options.whyWrong: Locale quirks do not matter here; any value outside the set falls back to the literal "ASC".

options.label: Bind sortBy as a placeholder: ORDER BY ? and ps.setString(2, sortBy).
options.whyWrong: Placeholders bind values, not identifiers. The database would sort by a constant string, so sorting breaks and the design is wrong.

options.label: Map sortBy through a fixed allowlist of column names and use the mapped constant, defaulting to name.
Strip semicolons, quotes and comment markers from sortBy before concatenating it.
options.whyWrong: Blacklisting is bypassable. A subquery inside CASE WHEN needs none of those characters, so blind injection still works.

options.label: Reject sortBy values longer than 30 characters.
options.whyWrong: A length cap does not restrict content. Short payloads such as (SELECT 1/0) or IF(...) still inject.

training.exploit: The attacker requests /products?category=tools&sortBy=(CASE WHEN (SELECT SUBSTR(password,1,1) FROM users WHERE username='admin')='a' THEN name ELSE price END). If the first character matches, results come back sorted by name; otherwise by price. By watching the row order, the attacker extracts data one character per request (boolean-based blind SQL injection), even though the WHERE clause is parameterized.

hints.line: Which part of the query is built by string concatenation rather than bound with a placeholder?
hints.bugClass: Untrusted text becomes part of a database query's structure.
hints.why: Think about what a PreparedStatement can and cannot bind.
hints.fix: Identifiers cannot be parameters, so you must choose from values you control.

writeup.summary: The category filter uses a bound parameter and the limit is clamped to an int, but the sort column is concatenated directly into the query. Prepared statements only protect values, not identifiers or clauses, so a caller can inject arbitrary SQL expressions into ORDER BY. Even without UNION, CASE and subqueries give a blind data-extraction oracle through result ordering. The fix is to map the user's choice to a fixed set of known column names and never pass user text into the clause. Blacklist filters and length caps are bypassable, and a placeholder cannot stand in for a column name.
